claim: GPR88 is an orphan G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) considered as a promising therapeutic target for neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: GPR88 is an orphan G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) considered as a promising therapeutic target for neuropsychiatric disorders; its pharmacology, however, remains scarcely understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the classification and potential therapeutic relevance of GPR88, supported by the broader scientific context presented in the manuscript.

claim: GPR88 inhibits the activation of both G protein- and β-arrestin-dependent signaling pathways of opioid receptors.
source: Based on our previous report of increased delta opioid receptor activity in Gpr88 null mice, we investigated the impact of GPR88 co-expression on the signaling of opioid receptors in vitro and revealed that GPR88 inhibits the activation of both their G protein- and β-arrestin-dependent signaling pathways.
evidence: The manuscript describes in vitro experiments showing GPR88's inhibitory effects on opioid receptor signaling pathways.

claim: In Gpr88 knockout mice, morphine-induced locomotor sensitization was facilitated.
source: In Gpr88 knockout mice, morphine-induced locomotor sensitization, withdrawal and supra-spinal analgesia were facilitated, consistent with a tonic inhibitory action of GPR88 on µOR signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments comparing Gpr88 knockout mice to wild-type controls.

claim: In Gpr88 knockout mice, morphine-induced withdrawal was facilitated.
source: In Gpr88 knockout mice, morphine-induced locomotor sensitization, withdrawal and supra-spinal analgesia were facilitated, consistent with a tonic inhibitory action of GPR88 on µOR signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments comparing Gpr88 knockout mice to wild-type controls.

claim: In Gpr88 knockout mice, morphine-induced supra-spinal analgesia was facilitated.
source: In Gpr88 knockout mice, morphine-induced locomotor sensitization, withdrawal and supra-spinal analgesia were facilitated, consistent with a tonic inhibitory action of GPR88 on µOR signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments comparing Gpr88 knockout mice to wild-type controls.

claim: GPR88 can decrease the G protein-dependent signaling of most receptors in close proximity.
source: We then explored GPR88 interactions with more striatal versus non-neuronal GPCRs, and revealed that GPR88 can decrease the G protein-dependent signaling of most receptors in close proximity, but impedes β-arrestin recruitment by all receptors tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro BRET and functional assays testing multiple GPCRs.

claim: GPR88 impedes β-arrestin recruitment by all receptors tested.
source: We then explored GPR88 interactions with more striatal versus non-neuronal GPCRs, and revealed that GPR88 can decrease the G protein-dependent signaling of most receptors in close proximity, but impedes β-arrestin recruitment by all receptors tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro BRET and functional assays testing multiple GPCRs.

claim: GPR88 expression varies over development in the brain of rodents, monkeys and humans.
source: GPR88 is a striatal-enriched orphan G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) whose expression varies over development in the brain of rodents, monkeys and humans (Ghate et al., 2007; Massart et al., 2009; Van Waes et al., 2011; Massart et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and schizophrenia.
source: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and several psychiatric, neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, speech delay and chorea (Alkufri et al., 2016; Del Zompo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to gene association studies.

claim: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and bipolar disorder.
source: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and several psychiatric, neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, speech delay and chorea (Alkufri et al., 2016; Del Zompo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to gene association studies.

claim: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and speech delay.
source: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and several psychiatric, neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, speech delay and chorea (Alkufri et al., 2016; Del Zompo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to gene association studies.

claim: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and chorea.
source: Gene association studies in humans have uncovered a link between GPR88 function and several psychiatric, neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, speech delay and chorea (Alkufri et al., 2016; Del Zompo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to gene association studies.

claim: Gpr88 gene transcript levels were found modified following exposure to mood stabilizers.
source: In rodents, transcript levels of Gpr88 gene were found modified following exposure to various psychoactive drugs, such as mood stabilizers, antidepressants, methamphetamine, L-DOPA and drugs of abuse (Conti et al., 2007; Ogden et al., 2004; Brandish et al., 2005; Le Merrer et al., 2012; Becker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of the Gpr88 gene in mice alters primarily striatal physiology.
source: In mice, deletion of the Gpr88 gene alters primarily striatal physiology, striatum-centered brain networks and striatal-dependent behaviors, with notably severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning, hyperactivity, stereotypies and altered reward-driven behaviors (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Meirsman et al., 2016b; Rainwater et al., 2017; Ben Hamida et al., 2018; Arefin et al., 2017; Quintana et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of the Gpr88 gene in mice causes severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning.
source: In mice, deletion of the Gpr88 gene alters primarily striatal physiology, striatum-centered brain networks and striatal-dependent behaviors, with notably severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning, hyperactivity, stereotypies and altered reward-driven behaviors (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Meirsman et al., 2016b; Rainwater et al., 2017; Ben Hamida et al., 2018; Arefin et al., 2017; Quintana et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of the Gpr88 gene in mice causes hyperactivity.
source: In mice, deletion of the Gpr88 gene alters primarily striatal physiology, striatum-centered brain networks and striatal-dependent behaviors, with notably severe deficits in motor coordination and skill learning, hyperactivity, stereotypies and altered reward-driven behaviors (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Meirsman et al., 2016b; Rainwater et al., 2017; Ben Hamida et al., 2018; Arefin et al., 2017; Quintana et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GPR88 is considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs.
source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classification studies.

claim: GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of the class A GPCR family.
source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classification studies.

claim: GPR88 displays an unusually short C-terminus of 14 amino acids.
source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
evidence: This is a structural characteristic of GPR88 based on sequence analysis.

claim: GPR88 displays a large non-homologous third intracellular loop of 67 amino acids.
source: Although considered as part of the class A (rhodopsin) family of GPCRs, GPR88 is distantly related to any well-known receptor of this class (Surgand et al., 2006; Vassilatis et al., 2003; Joost and Methner, 2002; Kakarala and Jamil, 2014) and displays an unusually short C-terminus (14 amino acids) and large non-homologous third intracellular loop (67 amino acids).
evidence: This is a structural characteristic of GPR88 based on sequence analysis.

claim: Based on the sequence of its putative transmembrane binding pocket, GPR88 clusters with class C GPCRs.
source: Moreover, based on the sequence of its putative transmembrane binding pocket, GPR88 clusters with class C GPCRs, for which the endogenous ligands bind in the large N-terminus domain (Surgand et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a classification study.

claim: Intensive efforts in deorphanizing GPR88 have remained vain.
source: Intensive efforts in deorphanizing GPR88 have remained vain (Bi et al., 2015; Decker et al., 2017; Dzierba et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2014); meanwhile, synthetic chemistry met significant difficulties in identifying potent agonists for this atypical receptor (Bi et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple deorphanization attempts.

claim: GPR88 was shown to display constitutive and ligand-induced activity on Gαi/o/z inhibitory protein coupling in heterologous and native cells.
source: Although this receptor was shown to display constitutive and ligand-induced activity on Gαi/o/z inhibitory protein coupling in heterologous and native cells (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Dzierba et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2018), its ability to recruit β-arrestins and intracellular trafficking have not been investigated yet.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ability of GPR88 to recruit β-arrestins and intracellular trafficking have not been investigated prior to this study.
source: Although this receptor was shown to display constitutive and ligand-induced activity on Gαi/o/z inhibitory protein coupling in heterologous and native cells (Meirsman et al., 2016a; Dzierba et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2018), its ability to recruit β-arrestins and intracellular trafficking have not been investigated yet.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study's investigations.

claim: Orphan GPCRs may influence the signaling of other GPCRs in a ligand-independent manner through hetero-oligomerization, as shown for GPR50.
source: Interestingly, it was proposed that orphan GPCRs may influence the signaling of other GPCRs in a ligand-independent manner through hetero-oligomerization, as shown for GPR50 (Levoye et al., 2006a; Levoye et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on GPR50.

claim: There was an increase in [35S]-GTPγS binding of striatal membranes from Gpr88-/- mice in response to stimulation by agonists of the muscarinic and opioid delta (δOR) and mu (μOR) receptors.
source: Remarkably, we have evidenced in a previous study (Meirsman et al., 2016a) an increase in [35S]-GTPγS binding of striatal membranes from Gpr88-/- mice in response to stimulation by agonists of the muscarinic and opioid delta (δOR) and mu (μOR) receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Behavioral features of Gpr88-/- mice intriguingly oppose several aspects of the phenotype of mice lacking δOR (Oprd1-/-).
source: Moreover, we noticed that behavioral features of these mutants intriguingly oppose several aspects of the phenotype of mice lacking δOR (Oprd1-/-) and that pharmacological blockade of δOR ameliorate behavioral deficits in Gpr88 knockout mice.
evidence: This is an observation from previous work comparing phenotypes.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of δOR ameliorates behavioral deficits in Gpr88 knockout mice.
source: Moreover, we noticed that behavioral features of these mutants intriguingly oppose several aspects of the phenotype of mice lacking δOR (Oprd1-/-) and that pharmacological blockade of δOR ameliorate behavioral deficits in Gpr88 knockout mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from previous work.

claim: GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with δOR, indicating close physical proximity.
source: We evidenced that GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with the three opioid receptors, δOR, κOR and µOR, indicative of close physical proximity (within 10 nm) to them, in addition to itself (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with κOR, indicating close physical proximity.
source: We evidenced that GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with the three opioid receptors, δOR, κOR and µOR, indicative of close physical proximity (within 10 nm) to them, in addition to itself (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with µOR, indicating close physical proximity.
source: We evidenced that GPR88 displays specific and saturated BRET signals when co-expressed with the three opioid receptors, δOR, κOR and µOR, indicative of close physical proximity (within 10 nm) to them, in addition to itself (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GPR88 possibly forms hetero-oligomers with all opioid receptors.
source: These results indicate that GPR88 possibly forms hetero-oligomers with all opioid receptors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the BRET data showing close proximity.

claim: Growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced δOR inhibition of cAMP accumulation.
source: While δOR cell surface expression (measured using anti-HA antibody, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) remained constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced δOR inhibition of cAMP accumulation (Gαi/o-dependent pathway) and β-arrestin2 (β−arr2) recruitment (and similarly β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claim: Growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced β-arrestin2 recruitment at δOR.
source: While δOR cell surface expression (measured using anti-HA antibody, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) remained constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), growing levels of GPR88 expression led to a dose-dependent reduction in SNC80-induced δOR inhibition of cAMP accumulation (Gαi/o-dependent pathway) and β-arrestin2 (β−arr2) recruitment (and similarly β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claim: GPR88 expression interfered with δOR/β−arr2 interactions under stimulated conditions only.
source: We evidenced that the probability of β−arr2 recruitment at δOR was low under basal conditions and high when δOR was stimulated. GPR88 expression interfered with δOR/β−arr2 interactions under stimulated conditions only.
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET experiments measuring β-arrestin recruitment under different conditions.

claim: Co-expressing GPR88 with δOR is sufficient to affect G protein and β-arrestin dependent signaling pathways and trafficking of δOR.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that co-expressing GPR88 with δOR is sufficient to affect G protein and β-arrestin dependent signaling pathways and trafficking of the latter.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: GPR88 expression decreased U50488H-activated κOR pathway to Gαi/o, although to a lesser extent than for δOR.
source: GPR88 expression decreased U50488H-activated κOR pathway to Gαi/o, although in our hands to a lesser extent than for δOR (decrease up to 27.7% of maximal effect versus 61.1% for δOR) and only for the highest dose of GPR88 cDNA, without altering κOR cell surface expression Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative dose-response experiments.

claim: GPR88 had a significant inhibitory effect on agonist-induced β−arr2 recruitment at κOR.
source: GPR88, however, had a significant inhibitory effect on agonist-induced β−arr2 recruitment at κOR (and β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by β-arrestin recruitment experiments.

claim: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-activated Gαi/o pathway of µOR.
source: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-activated Gαi/o pathway and β−arr2 recruitment of µOR (see also β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), µOR expression remaining stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claim: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-induced β−arr2 recruitment of µOR.
source: GPR88 expression had a significant dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DAMGO-activated Gαi/o pathway and β−arr2 recruitment of µOR (see also β−arr1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), µOR expression remaining stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in figures.

claim: Expressing GPR88 reduced the affinity of β−arr2 for DAMGO-stimulated µOR to that measured under basal conditions.
source: Focusing on β−arr2/µOR interactions, we observed again that β−arr2 had significantly more affinity for µOR under stimulated versus basal conditions. Expressing GPR88 reduced the affinity of β−arr2 for DAMGO-stimulated µOR to that measured under basal conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET experiments measuring β-arrestin affinity.

claim: DAMGO-induced µOR stimulation produced an increase in the phospho-ERK/total ERK ratio that was suppressed in the presence of GPR88.
source: We verified that DAMGO-induced µOR stimulation produced an increase in the phospho-ERK/total ERK total (pERK/tERK) ratio that was suppressed in the presence of GPR88 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pertussis toxin markedly reduced the early phase of DAMGO-induced phosphorylation of ERK, showing its dependence on G protein recruitment (Gi/o).
source: Addition of pertussis toxin (PTX) markedly reduced the early phase of DAMGO-induced phosphorylation of ERK, showing its dependence on G protein recruitment (Gi/o).
evidence: This claim is supported by PTX treatment experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GPR88 expression completely blocked DAMGO-induced phosphorylation of ERK.
source: PTX, however, failed to suppress a later phase of DAMGO-induced response, while GPR88 expression did (Figure 2B) (see gels in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The inhibitory effect of GPR88 on µOR signaling weakens when µOR amounts increase, with a complete restoration for high doses of µOR.
source: We showed that the inhibitory effect of GPR88 on µOR signaling weakens when µOR amounts increase, with a complete restoration for high doses of µOR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Increasing the amount of µOR was not able to completely overcome the inhibitory effect of GPR88 on β-arr2 recruitment at µOR.
source: In contrast, increasing the amount of µOR was not able to completely overcome the inhibitory effect of GPR88 (30 ng of cDNA) on β-arr2 recruitment at µOR; notably, no further recruitment was observed over 50 ng of µOR cDNA transfected.
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GPR88 inhibitory action on G-protein dependent µOR signaling was more sensitive to µOR level of expression than its blunting effects on β-arrestin recruitment.
source: In conclusion, GPR88 inhibitory action on G-protein dependent µOR signaling was more sensitive to µOR level of expression than its blunting effects on β-arrestin recruitment, suggesting different mechanisms of interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of varying µOR expression on different signaling pathways.

claim: Morphine injections induced a significant rise in locomotor activity that progressively sensitized upon repeated administration in both Gpr88-/- and Gpr88+/+ mice.
source: In both mouse lines, morphine injections induced a significant rise in locomotor activity that progressively sensitized upon repeated administration (Figure 3A, panel a).
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Locomotor activation and sensitization were markedly exacerbated in Gpr88-/- compared to Gpr88+/+ mice.
source: Locomotor activation and sensitization, however, were markedly exacerbated in Gpr88-/- compared to Gpr88+/+ mice (panel b).
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Gpr88 deletion facilitates morphine-induced locomotion and sensitization.
source: These results thus indicate that Gpr88 deletion facilitates morphine-induced locomotion and sensitization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the locomotor activity experiments.

claim: Gpr88-/- mice lost more body weight than controls upon exposure to escalating doses of morphine.
source: Upon exposure to escalating doses of morphine (n = 6 per treatment and genotype), Gpr88-/- lost more body weight than controls (panel a; Treatment: F1,20=43.7, p=0.0000; Day: F4,80=13.6, p=0.0000; Day x Genotype: F4,80=5.1, p=0.001; Day x Treatment: F4,80=9.9, p=0.0000; body weight was measured daily upon morphine treatment)
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When withdrawal was triggered by acute naloxone administration, Gpr88-/- animals displayed sniffing episodes quicker than their Gpr88+/+ counterparts.
source: when withdrawal was triggered by acute naloxone administration (1 mg/kg), mutant animals displayed sniffing episodes (panel b; Genotype/Treatment: F1,20=25.5, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,20=23.1, p=0.0001; Time: F3,60=10.5, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype/Treatment: F3,60=9.3, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype x Treatment: F3,60=8.3, p=0.0001) and vegetative signs of withdrawal (panel c; Genotype: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Treatment: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Time: F3,60=14.4, p=0.0000) quicker than their Gpr88+/+ counterparts
evidence: This claim is supported by withdrawal experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gpr88-/- and Gpr88+/+ mice displayed similar final withdrawal scores.
source: when withdrawal was triggered by acute naloxone administration (1 mg/kg), mutant animals displayed sniffing episodes (panel b; Genotype/Treatment: F1,20=25.5, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,20=23.1, p=0.0001; Time: F3,60=10.5, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype/Treatment: F3,60=9.3, p=0.0000; Time x Genotype x Treatment: F3,60=8.3, p=0.0001) and vegetative signs of withdrawal (panel c; Genotype: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Treatment: F1,20=5.3, p=0.0324; Time: F3,60=14.4, p=0.0000) quicker than their Gpr88+/+ counterparts, despite similar final withdrawal scores (panel d; Treatment: F1,20=38.9, p=0.0000)
evidence: This claim is supported by withdrawal experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gpr88-/- mice acquired preference for a compartment associated to morphine administration similarly as Gpr88+/+ animals.
source: Gpr88-/-mice acquired preference for a compartment associated to morphine administration (10 mg/Kg) similarly as Gpr88+/+ animals (panel a; Treatment: F1,28=45.8, p=0.0000; Conditioning: F1,28=15.7, p=0.0005; Conditioning x Treatment: F1,28=31.1, p=0.0000)
evidence: This claim is supported by CPP experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gpr88-/- mice extinguished morphine place preference conditioning quicker than wild-type counterparts.
source: they extinguished this conditioning quicker than wild-type counterparts (panel b; Genotype: F1,28=10.3, p=0034; Treatment: F1,28=6.5, p=0166; Genotype x Treatment: F1,28=5.0, p=0329; Session: F9,252=5.2, p=0.0000; Session x Treatment: F9,252=3.7, p=0.0002)
evidence: This claim is supported by CPP extinction experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gpr88-/- and Gpr88+/+ mice reinstated morphine place preference at comparable levels.
source: and finally reinstated morphine place preference at comparable levels as the latter (panel c; Treatment: F1,28=9.2, p=0.0052)
evidence: This claim is supported by CPP reinstatement experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gpr88-/- mice were significantly less sensitive to morphine analgesia at 48°C and 52°C in the tail flick test.
source: In the tail flick test (n = 7–9 per treatment and genotype), Gpr88-/- mice were significantly less sensitive to morphine analgesia at 48°C and 52°C (Genotype: F1,83=22.0, p=0.0000; Treatment: F1,83=84.9, p=0.0000; Temperature: F2,83=162.5, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,83=15.9, p=0.0001; Treatment x Temperature: F2,83=5.4, p=0.0065)
evidence: This claim is supported by tail immersion test experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the hot plate test, morphine-induced analgesia measured by increased jumping latency was increased in Gpr88 null mice versus controls.
source: in the hot plate test (n = 15–16 per treatment and genotype), morphine-induced analgesia was detected by increased jumping latency in treated animals (right panel); this effect was increased in Gpr88 null mice versus controls (Treatment: F1,59=79.7, p=0.0000; Genotype x Treatment: F1,59=4.0, p=0.0490)
evidence: This claim is supported by hot plate test experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Pharmacological activation of GPR88 by Compound 19 drastically reduced morphine-induced locomotor activity but left the amplitude of sensitization unchanged.
source: Exposure to morphine (IP, 10 mg/kg) induced an increase in locomotor activity that sensitized upon repeated administration in both vehicle and Compound 19-treated groups (panel a); pharmacological activation of GPR88 drastically reduced morphine-induced locomotor activity but left the amplitude of sensitization unchanged (Morphine effect: F1,30=305.1, p=0.0000; Compound 19: F1,30=55.3, p=0.0000; Day: F2,60=33.1, p=0.0000; Day x Morphine: F2,60=31.6, p=0.0000; Day x Morphine x Compound 19: F2,60=2.1, NS)
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity experiments with Compound 19 shown in Figure 3F.

claim: GPR88 displayed saturated BRET signals with all tested striatal GPCRs except the dopamine D1 receptor.
source: Remarkably, GPR88 displayed saturated BRET signals with all tested striatal GPCRs except the dopamine D1 receptor (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BRET signal between GPR88 and V2R was unsaturated.
source: In contrast, BRET signal was unsaturated for interactions with the two GPCRs identified as not expressed in CNS neurons, V2R and CXCR4 receptors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BRET signal between GPR88 and CXCR4 was unsaturated.
source: In contrast, BRET signal was unsaturated for interactions with the two GPCRs identified as not expressed in CNS neurons, V2R and CXCR4 receptors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET saturation experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GPR88 appears to possibly form hetero-oligomers with multiple GPCRs in addition to opioid receptors, notably those GPCRs whose expression is enriched in striatal regions.
source: Thus GPR88 appears to possibly form hetero-oligomers with multiple GPCRs in addition to opioid receptors, notably those GPCRs whose expression is enriched in striatal regions, where GPR88 is also the most expressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from BRET experiments and knowledge of expression patterns.

claim: Increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of dopamine D2 receptor.
source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of muscarinic M1 receptor.
source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of muscarinic M4 receptor.
source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GPR88 co-expression did not interfere with the G protein mediated signaling of adenosine A2A receptor.
source: Interestingly, increasing amounts of GPR88 expression interfered with the G protein mediated signaling of all GPCRs from which it comes close (dopamine D2 and muscarinic M1 and M4) except for the adenosine A2A receptor (Figure 5A, panels a,c,d,e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-expressing GPR88 with dopamine D1 receptor had no significant effect on D1 G protein dependent signaling, or even increased this signaling.
source: In contrast, co-expressing GPR88 with receptors for which we failed to evidence proximity to it, namely dopamine D1, vasopressin V2R and chemokine CXCR4 receptors, had no significant effect on their G protein dependent signaling, or even increased this signaling (D1 receptor) (Figure 5A, panels b,g,h).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GPR88 expression markedly blunted CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment under both basal and stimulated conditions.
source: Moreover, GPR88 expression markedly blunted CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment under both basal and stimulated conditions (Figure 5B, panel h).
evidence: This claim is supported by β-arrestin recruitment assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GPR88 co-expression inhibits G protein dependent signaling of most GPCRs from which it comes close, and only these.
source: GPR88 co-expression was able to inhibit G protein dependent signaling of most GPCRs from which it comes close, and only these.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on functional assays across multiple GPCRs.

claim: GPR88 co-expression resulted in blunted β-arrestin recruitment by all GPCRs tested.
source: In contrast, such co-expression resulted in blunted β-arrestin recruitment by all GPCRs tested.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on β-arrestin recruitment assays across multiple GPCRs.

claim: CXCR4 co-expression had no deleterious effect on DAMGO-induced µOR signaling on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways.
source: Consistent with no detected proximity, CXCR4 co-expression had no deleterious effect on DAMGO-induced µOR signaling, and conversely µOR co-expression did not modify SDF1-mediated CXCR4 signaling, on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: µOR co-expression did not modify SDF1-mediated CXCR4 signaling on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways.
source: Consistent with no detected proximity, CXCR4 co-expression had no deleterious effect on DAMGO-induced µOR signaling, and conversely µOR co-expression did not modify SDF1-mediated CXCR4 signaling, on either the G protein- or β-arrestin-dependent pathways (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: κOR expression repressed agonist-mediated G protein activation and β-arr2 recruitment by µOR, with which it forms hetero-oligomers.
source: In contrast, κOR expression repressed agonist-mediated G protein activation and β-arr2 recruitment by µOR, with which it forms hetero-oligomers (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: κOR expression had no significant impact on G protein-mediated signaling by CXCR4 but significantly inhibited β-arr2-dependent recruitment by this receptor.
source: Such expression however had no significant impact on G protein-mediated signaling by CXCR4 but significantly inhibited β-arr2-dependent recruitment by this receptor (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GPR88 had a more significant inhibitory impact on G protein dependent µOR signaling than κOR.
source: Compared to κOR, GPR88 had a more significant inhibitory impact on G protein dependent µOR signaling but similarly blunted µOR-dependent β-arr2 recruitment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative functional assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GPR88 was able to repress CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment more than κOR, despite no detectable physical proximity to CXCR4.
source: Finally, although GPR88 had little influence on SDF1-induced G protein activation by CXCR4 (see also Figure 5G), it was able to repress CXCR4-dependent β-arr2 recruitment more than κOR, despite no detectable physical proximity to CXCR4 (Figures 4B and 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative functional assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GPR88 can interfere with the signaling of other GPCRs when coming in close vicinity of them, but also in the absence of detected proximity.
source: Together, these results indicate that GPR88 can interfere with the signaling of other GPCRs when coming in close vicinity of them, but also in the absence of detected proximity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on functional assays comparing GPCRs with and without proximity to GPR88.

claim: The probability that β-arr2 was recruited at GPR88 and CXCR4 in the absence of pharmacological stimulation was higher than at the two opioid receptors.
source: The probability that β-arr2 was recruited at GPR88 and CXCR4 in the absence of pharmacological stimulation was higher than at the two opioid receptors (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by basal β-arrestin recruitment experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: GPR88 displays a significant, patchy, intracellular distribution, suggesting its presence in vesicular compartments.
source: We observed, in addition to location at cell membrane, a significant, patchy, intracellular distribution of GPR88 (Figure 6Ea), suggesting its presence in vesicular compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: β-arr2 was found colocalized with GPR88-expressing patches and appeared depleted around the brightest ones, suggesting sequestration by GPR88.
source: Diffuse cytosolic distribution of β-arr2 (Figure 6Eb) was found colocalized with GPR88-expressing patches (Figure 6Ec) and appeared depleted around the brightest ones (framed, arrow head), suggesting sequestration by GPR88.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: GPR88 can bias the signaling of other GPCRs independently from oligomerization, possibly by trapping β-arrestins in intracellular compartments.
source: Thus, GPR88 can bias the signaling of other GPCRs independently from oligomerization, possibly by trapping β-arrestins in intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: µOR and κOR closely interact, as previously reported.
source: Indeed, we verified that µOR and κOR closely interact (Figure 6C, upper panel), as previously reported (Fujita et al., 2014), and evidenced that CXCR4 likely forms hetero-oligomers with κOR but not µOR (Figure 6C, middle and right panels, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET experiments shown in Figure 6C and citation to previous work.

claim: CXCR4 likely forms hetero-oligomers with κOR but not µOR.
source: Indeed, we verified that µOR and κOR closely interact (Figure 6C, upper panel), as previously reported (Fujita et al., 2014), and evidenced that CXCR4 likely forms hetero-oligomers with κOR but not µOR (Figure 6C, middle and right panels, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRET experiments shown in Figure 6C.
